title: Poliomyelitis
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Poliomyelitis is an acute, non‑contagious viral infection that attacks anterior horn cells, causing asymmetric flaccid paralysis. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on clinical features and simple laboratory tests; management is supportive with early respiratory support.

sections.p: Poliomyelitis is caused by the enterovirus type 1, 2 or 3, transmitted faecal‑oral route. It is largely controlled by vaccination but outbreaks still occur in areas with low coverage.
The virus is a non‑enveloped, single‑stranded RNA virus of the Picornaviridae family. It has a tropism for motor neurons in the anterior horn of the spinal cord.
b: No cell culture needed for diagnosis

sections.p: Transmission is faecal‑oral; contaminated water or food is common in low‑resource settings. The virus replicates in the gut, spreads hematogenously to the CNS.
The hallmark is asymmetric flaccid paralysis of limbs, often with bulbar involvement. Sensory nerves are spared, distinguishing it from spinal cord lesions.
Clinical diagnosis is based on history of recent infection and asymmetric flaccid paralysis. Laboratory confirmation is rarely needed in resource‑poor settings.
b: CSF: normal cell count, normal protein

t.b: Positive IgM in serum or CSF

sections.p: There is no antiviral therapy; care focuses on supportive measures, early recognition of respiratory compromise and vaccination.
b: Early intubation if respiratory muscle weakness

sections.p: Remember that poliomyelitis presents with flaccid paralysis without sensory loss and that respiratory failure is the main cause of death.
Other causes of acute flaccid paralysis include Guillain‑Barré syndrome, transverse myelitis, and spinal cord compression.
b: GBS: ascending weakness, areflexia, sensory changes

sections.p: CSF protein may be mildly elevated in early polio; normal CSF does not exclude polio.
b: Normal CSF does not rule out polio

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, monitor respiratory function, and ensure early vaccination of contacts.
Urgent referral if respiratory distress, rapid progression of weakness, or loss of consciousness.

faq.q: What is the most common age group affected by poliomyelitis?
faq.a: Children under 5 years are most vulnerable, especially in areas with low vaccination coverage.

faq.q: Can poliomyelitis be transmitted from person to person?
faq.a: Yes, via the faecal‑oral route; it is not airborne.

faq.q: What is the main reason for death in polio patients?
faq.a: Respiratory failure due to paralysis of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles.

exam: A 3‑year‑old presents with sudden onset of right leg weakness and normal sensation – what is the most likely diagnosis? — Asymmetric flaccid paralysis with preserved sensation points to poliomyelitis.
A child with suspected polio develops respiratory distress – what is the first step in management? — Early intubation and mechanical ventilation to support diaphragm function.
Which laboratory test would confirm acute poliomyelitis if available? — Serum or CSF IgM against poliovirus.
Why is a normal CSF cell count not sufficient to rule out polio? — Polio can have normal or mildly elevated CSF; clinical picture is paramount.
What is the most important public health measure to prevent polio outbreaks? — Routine immunisation with IPV or OPV.
A patient with acute flaccid paralysis has normal reflexes – what condition should be considered? — Guillain‑Barré syndrome typically has areflexia; preserved reflexes suggest polio.
